question: Under Tennessee's Real Estate Broker License Act, how may an agency or subagency relationship be created?
choice_a: By verbal agreement between the licensee and a party
choice_b: Automatically once a licensee shows a property to a buyer
choice_c: By implication from the parties' course of dealing
choice_d: Only through a specific written bilateral agreement establishing the terms and conditions of the relationship
explanation: T.C.A. 62-13-401 expressly states that an agency or subagency relationship 'shall not be assumed, implied or created' without a specific written bilateral agreement establishing its terms -- Tennessee does not recognize implied agency for real estate licensees.
source_note: T.C.A. 62-13-401, Creation of agency relationship, Tennessee Real Estate Broker License Act of 1973.

question: Under Tennessee law, if a real estate licensee has not entered into a written agency agreement with a party, what is the licensee's status by default?
choice_a: A facilitator, who is not considered an agent or advocate of any party to the transaction
choice_b: An implied general agent of the buyer
choice_c: A subagent of the listing broker automatically
choice_d: A dual agent by default
explanation: T.C.A. 62-13-401 provides that until a licensee enters into a specific written agreement to establish agency, the licensee is considered a facilitator and is not treated as an agent or advocate for any party.

question: Under Tennessee law, which action creates an agency relationship between a licensee and a seller?
choice_a: The licensee simply placing a for-sale sign on the property
choice_b: The seller executing an exclusive agency listing agreement or exclusive right to sell listing agreement with the licensee's firm
choice_c: The seller mentioning to the licensee that they'd like to sell
choice_d: The licensee showing the property to a prospective buyer
explanation: T.C.A. 62-13-401 specifically identifies execution of either an exclusive agency listing agreement or an exclusive right to sell listing agreement as creating an agency relationship with the seller.

question: Under T.C.A. 62-13-402, a Tennessee real estate licensee who is engaged as an agent serves in what capacity?
choice_a: A universal agent with unrestricted authority over the client's affairs
choice_b: A general agent responsible for the client's entire financial portfolio
choice_c: A limited agent retained to provide real estate services to a client
choice_d: A guarantor of the transaction's outcome
explanation: T.C.A. 62-13-402(a) defines a Tennessee real estate licensee acting as an agent as a 'limited agent' retained to provide real estate services, with statutorily defined duties rather than open-ended, unlimited authority.

question: Under Tennessee law, the duties enumerated in T.C.A. 62-13-403 and 62-13-404 have what effect on a licensee's obligations to a client?
choice_a: They apply only in addition to, but never in place of, common law fiduciary duties
choice_b: They apply only to commercial transactions
choice_c: They have no legal effect and are merely advisory best practices
choice_d: They supersede any fiduciary or common law duties a licensee would otherwise owe, as of January 1, 1996
explanation: T.C.A. 62-13-402(c) states that the duties in 62-13-403 and 62-13-404 superseded any fiduciary or common law duties owed by a licensee to a client, effective January 1, 1996, establishing a statutory (rather than pure common-law) duty framework in Tennessee.

question: Under T.C.A. 62-13-405, when must a Tennessee licensee confirm agency status disclosure in writing with an unrepresented buyer?
choice_a: Prior to the preparation of an offer to purchase
choice_b: Only after the offer has been accepted
choice_c: At closing
choice_d: Within 30 days after the property is listed
explanation: T.C.A. 62-13-405 requires that the disclosure of agency status be confirmed in writing with an unrepresented buyer prior to the preparation of an offer to purchase, ensuring the buyer understands the licensee's role before submitting an offer.

question: Under T.C.A. 62-13-405, when must written confirmation of agency status be provided to an unrepresented seller?
choice_a: Only at the closing table
choice_b: Prior to execution of a listing agreement or presentation of an offer to purchase, whichever occurs first
choice_c: Within 10 days after the property sells
choice_d: There is no specific timing requirement for sellers
explanation: T.C.A. 62-13-405 requires written confirmation of agency status disclosure to an unrepresented seller before execution of a listing agreement or presentation of an offer to purchase, whichever comes first.

question: After providing the required written agency disclosure under Tennessee law, what must the licensee obtain from the party?
choice_a: A notarized affidavit of understanding
choice_b: A verbal confirmation recorded on the licensee's phone
choice_c: A signed receipt acknowledging delivery of the disclosure
choice_d: Nothing further is required after delivery
explanation: T.C.A. 62-13-405 requires the licensee to obtain a signed receipt for the disclosure from the party to whom it was provided, documenting that the disclosure was actually delivered.

question: What must the signed disclosure receipt under T.C.A. 62-13-405 include, in addition to acknowledgment of the disclosure itself?
choice_a: The exact commission percentage to be paid at closing
choice_b: The buyer's Social Security number for identification
choice_c: A waiver of the party's right to file any future complaint
choice_d: A statement that the party was informed of the applicable complaint-filing deadline and the address and telephone number of the Tennessee Real Estate Commission
explanation: T.C.A. 62-13-405 requires the receipt to state that the party was informed that any complaint alleging a violation must be filed within the applicable statute of limitations, along with the Tennessee Real Estate Commission's address and telephone number.
source_note: T.C.A. 62-13-405; see also T.C.A. 62-13-312 (discipline provisions) and 62-13-313(e) (statute of limitations).

question: Under Tennessee law, does the written agency status disclosure required by T.C.A. 62-13-405 itself create an agency relationship?
choice_a: No -- it is not a substitute for the specific written agreement required to establish an actual agency relationship under 62-13-406
choice_b: Yes -- signing the disclosure automatically creates a full agency relationship
choice_c: Yes, but only for buyer clients
choice_d: Yes, but only if the licensee is a designated agent
explanation: T.C.A. 62-13-405 expressly clarifies that the written disclosure requirement is not to be construed as, or considered a substitute for, a written agreement establishing an agency relationship as referenced in 62-13-406; disclosure and agency creation are distinct requirements.

question: Under T.C.A. 62-13-403, a Tennessee licensee owes which duty to all parties in a transaction, including non-clients?
choice_a: The duty of undivided loyalty owed only to a fiduciary client
choice_b: The duty to disclose adverse facts about the property that are actually known to the licensee
choice_c: The duty to negotiate exclusively for the highest possible price for whichever party pays commission
choice_d: No duty exists toward a party the licensee does not represent
explanation: T.C.A. 62-13-403 requires a licensee to disclose to all parties any adverse facts actually known by the licensee, regardless of whether the licensee represents that party as a client.
source_note: T.C.A. 62-13-403, Duty owed to all parties.

question: T.C.A. 62-13-403 requires a Tennessee licensee to provide services to each party to a transaction with:
choice_a: Absolute loyalty regardless of who the client is
choice_b: Complete confidentiality toward every party, including the licensee's own client
choice_c: Honesty and good faith
choice_d: No specific standard of conduct
explanation: T.C.A. 62-13-403 obligates a licensee to provide services to every party to the transaction -- client and non-client alike -- with honesty and good faith, a baseline standard distinct from the higher fiduciary duties owed only to clients.

question: Under T.C.A. 62-13-403, a Tennessee licensee must maintain confidentiality of a party's information under what circumstance?
choice_a: Only after the transaction closes
choice_b: Confidentiality is never required toward non-client parties
choice_c: Only if the party specifically requests confidentiality in writing
choice_d: Until a written agency agreement disclosing representation has been made
explanation: T.C.A. 62-13-403 requires a licensee to maintain the confidentiality of information received from any party until a written agency agreement is disclosed, protecting parties before it becomes clear who the licensee actually represents.

question: Under T.C.A. 62-13-403, if requested, a licensee must provide which type of information to a party?
choice_a: Timely and accurate information about market conditions that is a matter of public record
choice_b: The licensee's personal opinion on where property values will be in ten years
choice_c: Confidential appraisal information belonging to another client
choice_d: Legal advice regarding the enforceability of the contract
explanation: T.C.A. 62-13-403 requires licensees to share timely and accurate public-record-based market condition data with a party upon request, without requiring the licensee to render legal advice or reveal another client's confidential information.

question: Under T.C.A. 62-13-403, a Tennessee licensee's duty regarding trust fund deposits and other property received requires the licensee to:
choice_a: Keep trust funds in the licensee's personal operating account for convenience
choice_b: Timely account for trust fund deposits and all other property received in the transaction
choice_c: Disburse trust funds immediately to whichever party the licensee represents
choice_d: Wait until the transaction closes to account for any funds received
explanation: T.C.A. 62-13-403 requires licensees to timely account for trust fund deposits and other property received, a duty owed to all parties regardless of representation, consistent with broader trust account and escrow handling requirements.

question: Under T.C.A. 62-13-403, if a Tennessee licensee has a personal interest in a transaction (such as wanting to purchase a property they have listed), the licensee must:
choice_a: Keep the interest private since it does not affect the transaction
choice_b: Have a relative complete the transaction without disclosure
choice_c: Disclose that personal interest to the affected party
choice_d: Disclose the interest only if directly asked
explanation: T.C.A. 62-13-403 prohibits undisclosed self-dealing and requires disclosure when a licensee has a personal interest in a transaction, ensuring parties can evaluate the licensee's objectivity before proceeding.

question: If a Tennessee licensee refers a client to an affiliated title company or lender and expects to receive compensation for that referral, T.C.A. 62-13-403 requires the licensee to:
choice_a: Keep the referral arrangement confidential as a trade secret
choice_b: Refuse any compensation regardless of disclosure
choice_c: Disclose the arrangement only after closing
choice_d: Disclose the financial relationship and expectation of compensation to the party being referred
explanation: T.C.A. 62-13-403 requires disclosure when a licensee refers a party to a service provider in which the licensee has a financial interest or from which the licensee expects to receive referral compensation, addressing potential conflicts of interest.

question: A Tennessee licensee representing a seller wants to submit an offer to purchase the listed property through an LLC the licensee owns. Under Tennessee's agency and disclosure requirements, the licensee must:
choice_a: Fully disclose the licensee's ownership interest in the purchasing entity to the seller before proceeding
choice_b: Purchase the property without disclosure since the LLC is a separate legal entity
choice_c: Resign the listing without any explanation to the seller
choice_d: Only disclose the interest to the buyer's agent, not the seller
explanation: Disclosure obligations under T.C.A. 62-13-403 apply regardless of how a licensee structures a personal purchase; using an LLC does not eliminate the duty to disclose the licensee's beneficial interest in the transaction to the seller.

question: Under T.C.A. 62-13-404, a licensee's duty of assistance to a client includes which obligation regarding offers?
choice_a: Screening out offers the licensee personally believes are too low before showing them to the client
choice_b: Receiving all offers and counteroffers and forwarding them promptly to the client
choice_c: Forwarding offers only if they meet or exceed the listing price
choice_d: Waiting until multiple offers are received before presenting any to the client
explanation: T.C.A. 62-13-404(c) requires a licensee, as part of the duty of assistance to a client, to receive all offers and counteroffers and promptly forward them to the client -- a licensee cannot unilaterally decide which offers the client gets to see.
source_note: T.C.A. 62-13-404, Duty owed to licensee's client.

question: Beyond forwarding offers, T.C.A. 62-13-404's duty of assistance to a client also includes helping the client with which tasks, unless waived in writing?
choice_a: Providing formal legal representation in any resulting litigation
choice_b: Guaranteeing the transaction will close
choice_c: Arranging property showings and answering questions about negotiation within the licensee's expertise
choice_d: Personally financing the client's earnest money deposit
explanation: T.C.A. 62-13-404(c) lists assistance duties including arranging showings, answering negotiation questions within the licensee's expertise, and advising on forms, procedures, and closing steps, unless these duties are waived in writing by the client.

question: If a Tennessee client waives certain assistance duties under T.C.A. 62-13-404, what must the licensee ensure?
choice_a: The waiver is valid even if made only verbally
choice_b: The waived duties automatically transfer to the opposing party's agent
choice_c: No further documentation is needed once the client agrees verbally
choice_d: The client receives written notification that they cannot rely on another licensee to perform those specific waived services
explanation: T.C.A. 62-13-404 requires that if a client waives any assistance duties, the client must be given written notice that they cannot then expect another licensee to perform the waived services, ensuring the client understands the consequence of waiving those duties.

question: Under T.C.A. 62-13-406, designated agency allows a managing broker to do what?
choice_a: Appoint an individual licensee as the designated agent of one party, to the exclusion of all other licensees affiliated with that managing broker
choice_b: Require every licensee at the firm to jointly represent both the buyer and seller
choice_c: Automatically become a dual agent in every in-house transaction
choice_d: Prohibit any licensee in the firm from representing a buyer
explanation: T.C.A. 62-13-406 permits a managing broker to appoint a specific licensee as the designated and individual agent of a party, to the exclusion of all other licensees employed by or affiliated with that managing broker.

question: Under Tennessee's designated agency statute, what happens to knowledge or information held by one designated agent regarding their client?
choice_a: It must automatically be shared with the managing broker and the opposing designated agent
choice_b: It is not imputed to the other designated agent, the other client, or the managing broker
choice_c: It becomes public record
choice_d: It is imputed only if the transaction fails to close
explanation: T.C.A. 62-13-406 provides that there is no imputation of knowledge or information among or between clients, the managing broker, and any designated agent or agents, creating an information barrier that protects each client's confidentiality even though both designated agents work for the same firm.

question: How does Tennessee's designated agency framework help a managing broker avoid being classified as a dual agent when two in-house licensees represent opposing parties?
choice_a: The managing broker is always classified as a dual agent regardless of designation
choice_b: Designated agency requires the two parties to hire outside legal counsel instead
choice_c: Because each designated agent individually represents only one party's interests, and there is no imputation of knowledge between them, the managing broker is not deemed to represent both parties as a single dual agent
choice_d: Designated agency eliminates the need for either party to have any representation
explanation: T.C.A. 62-13-406 structures designated agency so that each individually appointed licensee represents only their assigned party's interests, with no imputed knowledge between them, allowing the managing broker's firm to have both sides represented without either designated agent -- or the firm as a whole -- being treated as a conflicted dual agent.

question: Under T.C.A. 62-13-406, does designating individual agents for the buyer and seller eliminate the managing broker's contractual rights under the listing agreement?
choice_a: Yes -- designation voids the original listing agreement entirely
choice_b: Yes -- the designated agent, not the firm, becomes the party to the listing agreement
choice_c: It depends on which party pays the commission
choice_d: No -- the managing broker retains contractual rights to any listing or advertising agreement between the firm and the property owner
explanation: T.C.A. 62-13-406 clarifies that designated agency does not eliminate the managing broker's contractual rights to any listing or advertising agreement between the firm and a property owner, even though an individual licensee has been designated to represent that owner.

question: Under T.C.A. 62-13-401, a Tennessee licensee acting as a facilitator (because no written agency agreement exists) has what relationship to the parties?
choice_a: The licensee is not considered an agent or advocate of any party to the transaction
choice_b: The licensee is automatically considered the buyer's agent
choice_c: The licensee owes full fiduciary duties to whichever party pays commission
choice_d: The licensee has no duties of honesty or fair dealing to anyone
explanation: T.C.A. 62-13-401 establishes that absent a written agency agreement, a licensee is a facilitator and is not considered an agent or advocate of any party -- though the licensee still owes baseline duties under 62-13-403.

question: Under T.C.A. 62-13-407, when may a client or party be held liable for damages arising from a licensee's misrepresentation made while acting as an agent, subagent, or facilitator?
choice_a: In all cases, regardless of the client's knowledge
choice_b: Only if the client or party knew or had reason to know of the misrepresentation
choice_c: Never, under any circumstances
choice_d: Only if the misrepresentation was made in writing
explanation: T.C.A. 62-13-407 protects a client or party from liability for a licensee's misrepresentations arising out of the licensee's services as agent, subagent, or facilitator, unless the client or party knew or had reason to know of the misrepresentation.

question: Compared to traditional dual agency (one licensee personally representing both the buyer and seller), how does Tennessee's designated agency statute change the typical in-house transaction structure?
choice_a: It bans in-house (same-firm) transactions entirely
choice_b: It requires the managing broker to personally handle every in-house transaction as a neutral facilitator
choice_c: It allows two separate licensees within the same firm to each individually represent one party, rather than requiring or defaulting to a single licensee representing both sides
choice_d: It has no effect on how in-house transactions are structured
explanation: Tennessee's designated agency framework under T.C.A. 62-13-406 provides an alternative to a single licensee acting as a true dual agent for both parties, instead allowing two separate individually-designated licensees within the same firm to each fully represent one party's interests.
